items.note: Author's assessment that the Udaypur temple escaped the fate of Vijay Mandir and is the 'Kohinoor' of ancient architecture of the area, yet left neglected.
items.gloss: It is fortunate that the Udaipur temple was spared such a fate. It is the Kohinoor of ancient Indian architecture in this region, yet it has been kept on a rubbish heap, and I am astonished that visiting officials keep leaving it that way.

items.note: States Vidisha's known history is two and a half thousand years old, a long rich cultural tradition.
items.gloss: The known history of Vidisha is two and a half thousand years old. It has a long, rich cultural tradition, but today's society retains not a trace of it.

items.note: Argues the issue is not only the palace (khasra no. 822) but renewing the whole of Udaypur, calling on district organisations to give a day each month.
items.gloss: This is not just about khasra number 822, the Udaipur palace. It is about giving new life to the whole of Udaipur; otherwise Udaipur will soon cease to exist. I believe all social and business organisations of the district should come together with open hearts and pockets, and give Udaipur one day every month.

items.note: Practical proposals: listen at old gateways, clear ruins and rubbish.
items.gloss: Put an ear to the ancient gates and doorways. Clean the ruins. Clear all kinds of rubbish.

items.note: Describes a goddess image with head severed, ten arms cut and feet struck off; attackers in some middle century damaged sculptures inside and outside the temple.
items.gloss: I was shaken, as if she were speaking. So that she could not speak, the attackers severed her head from her body; so she could not gesture, her ten arms were cut off; so she could not step out of the statue, even her feet were broken. In some intervening century attackers assaulted the temple and badly damaged the images inside and outside.

items.note: Two Arabic/Persian inscriptions on gateways built from temple fragments; Muhammad bin Tughlaq's name read, dated 1336-1338.
items.gloss: At the back of the temple two free-standing doorways, built from the temple's own broken pieces, carry two Arabic or Persian inscriptions. Dr Mishra had them read; Muhammad bin Tughlaq's name was clearly read in them. They date to 1336-1338.

claim.value: two Arabic/Persian inscriptions of 1336-1338 on rear doorways

items.note: Reads the Tughlaq inscription as sign of Tughlaq raiders at Udaypur when Paramara power was ending.
items.gloss: This is 258 years after King Udayavijay. The inscription points clearly to the presence of Tughlaq's raiders in Udaipur, who must have come to occupy and plunder the city. By then Paramara splendour was ending; Udaipur may have been the last city where Paramara kin kept resisting, since at Dhar and Mandu they were besieged and killed.

items.note: After the last Paramara king's death at Mandu, raiders spread to Udaypur; author calls the temple damage the first named evidence of foreign attack there (speculative 'must have' phrasing).
items.gloss: After the last Paramara king Mahlakdeva died at Mandu at the hands of Ainul Mulk Multani sent by Alauddin Khilji, bands of raiders must have begun to hover over other prosperous towns. Udaipur's guardians must have died in battle, left, or settled nearby. It is certain that surviving Paramara kin were then the feudatories, who must have faced Tughlaq's raiders. This is the first named evidence in Udaipur of foreign Muslim invaders damaging the temple.

items.note: Describes visible mutilation on goddess images today (breasts, noses, ears, faces).
items.gloss: Even today you can see the breasts and chests of goddess images, adorned with ornaments, cut off; noses and ears broken; faces disfigured.

items.note: Reads the Tughlaq inscription as witness that the temple was plundered; calls it the settlement's first acquaintance with Islam.
items.gloss: Here Tughlaq's inscription is witness that the temple must have been looted and surrounded to be broken. Plainly this was the settlement's first introduction to Islam.

items.note: Author concedes the single inscription does not legally prove Tughlaq did it; earlier raiders of Alauddin Khilji or Iltutmish may have struck.
items.gloss: In the language of law there is no direct proof against the killers. One inscription alone does not prove Muhammad Tughlaq did or had this done. It is possible that stray raiders of Alauddin Khilji or Shamsuddin Iltutmish attacked earlier, and equally possible that someone did so later.

items.note: Imagined narration of the temple's foundation ceremony attended by Udayaditya, feudatories and craftsmen from Dhara, Ujjain, Mandapadurga and Bhopal (literary reconstruction, not cited evidence).
items.gloss: The festival of bhumipujan, foundation-laying and abhisheka in the sanctum, when Maharaj Udayaditya himself was present with ministers and family. Many chief feudatories and craftsmen with their pupils came from Dhara city, Ujjayini, Mandapadurga and Bhopal.

items.note: Describes the town ringed by fort ramparts and a large reservoir built below the fort's west wall to supply caravans, farmers and pilgrims (literary reconstruction).
items.gloss: The beauty of this town, surrounded by the fort's ramparts, was to be enhanced. Below the fort's west wall a vast reservoir was being built, supplying water to passing military and merchant caravans, farmers and devotees.

items.note: Imagined account of craftsmen from Paramara workshops and architects' camp raising the temple.
items.gloss: Countless skilled artisans and workers came from the Paramara workshops to set the carved stones and images in place. Final instructions were given in the architects' camp, and the temple began to rise above ground.

items.note: Paramara kings were art-loving; temples built across the realm from Bhojpur to Dhara, Ujjayini, Mandapadurga and Omkareshwar; craftsmen busiest.
items.gloss: All kings of the Paramara dynasty were lovers of art. Temple construction went on across the kingdom: from the rock of Bhojpur to Dhara, Ujjayini, Mandapadurga and Omkareshwar. If anyone was busiest under Paramara rule it was the ideal craftsmen. They carved wonders in stone.

items.note: Narrated attack on the town; people hide on the hill; narrator supposes Kalachuris have taken over (fictional first-person voice).
items.gloss: Many people hid on the hill to save their lives. Groups of invaders filled the roads around the temple shouting strange slogans. Such conflicts were not new for kingdoms. We thought the town's new masters had come: the Paramaras would no longer be here. Perhaps the Kalachuris have taken over.

reject_reason: fictional first-person narration by a statue; no citable evidence
imaginative narration of image destruction; no datable or citable claim

items.note: Narrated: invaders built a wall behind the temple from its stones and set two inscriptions in two doorways, one naming Muhammad bin Tughlaq (imaginative narration echoing the epigraphic find).
items.gloss: Now they tried to build a wall behind the temple, breaking out all the stones from the temple itself. They made two inscriptions in their own language and fixed them in two doorways. One name I still remember: 'Mohammad bin Tughlaq'.

reject_reason: fictional first-person narration by a statue; no citable evidence

items.note: Claims Vijay Mandir at Vidisha was destroyed and the Sarasvati Kanthabharana at Dhara, Ujjain and Mandapadurga turned into mosques and tombs.
items.gloss: At Vidisha the splendour of Vijay Mandir was totally destroyed. History saw the Sarasvati Kanthabharanas of Dhara, Ujjain and Mandapadurga turned into places of worship and tombs. Great monuments of architecture became desolate mounds or ugly buildings.

items.note: Ruins of the ancient palace found carrying private-property boards; a tehsildar had to visit after a newspaper campaign (8 Jan 2021 post).
items.gloss: This is what was found at the ruins of Udaipur's ancient palace. The pictorial truth of Udaipur was tweeted to the Prime Minister, the Union tourism minister and the Chief Minister. The Patrika newspaper took up a campaign and a tehsildar had to visit the palace ruins.

items.note: Tehsildar states the palace spreading over three and a half bighas is, per revenue records, nobody's private property.
items.gloss: He says someone hung a private-property board on the gate yesterday and it has been removed. This palace spread over three and a half bighas is, according to revenue department records, not anyone's private property.

claim.value: revenue record: not private property (area 3.5 bigha)

items.note: A private claimant says Jahangir laid the palace's foundation, Shah Jahan completed it and gave it to the Qazi's family with 84 villages' qazi-ship.
items.gloss: The claimant said Jahangir laid the foundation stone of this palace in Udaipur. It was completed in Shah Jahan's time and given to the Qazi's family to lead prayers in the mosque. With it the qaziyat of 84 villages was also given to them.

claim.value: Jahangir laid foundation; Shah Jahan completed (claimant's account)

items.note: Dr Mishra's reasoning on the Mughal-grant claim of 84 villages' zamindari used to justify the private-property sign.
items.gloss: His argument: if Jahangir or Shah Jahan gave them this place and it is deemed private property, then by that claim the government would have to give them the 84 villages whose zamindari they say the Mughals granted. For the signboard claiming private ownership of the fort, they have only this Jahangir-Shah Jahan story.

reject_reason: rhetorical questions on identity and conversion; no citable evidence

items.note: Over twenty inscriptions on the stones of the temple's three doorways.
items.gloss: On the stones of the three doorways of King Udayaditya's temple of the Paramara dynasty there are more than twenty inscriptions that give important information about that time.

claim.value: more than twenty on the three doorways

items.note: Recommends the Collector visit and prepare an action plan for conserving every ancient monument of Udaypur before the next transfer.
items.gloss: I think the Collector should go and see for himself and not confine legal action to paper. A plan of action for conserving the ancient monuments of every corner of Udaipur should be made and implemented before the next transfer.

items.note: Calls on organisations, school and college groups and educational institutions to take part; the work cannot rest on one party.
items.gloss: Organisations that are now awake should shake their elected representatives and take a procession to Udaipur. School and college groups should keep arriving; educational institutions should run constructive campaigns. This work cannot be left to one party.

items.note: Dr Suresh Mishra: the whole of Udaipur could be developed as a heritage town.
items.gloss: Dr Suresh Mishra said while returning from Udaipur that the entire town could be developed like a heritage town. Our ancestors could not save Vijay Mandir; let us at least save Udaipur.

items.note: Officials' VIP darshan tradition at Nilakantheshwar; few notice the surroundings' neglect or the thousand years of known history.
items.gloss: Every SDM and tehsildar of Ganj Basoda wishes to bring the officer with family for darshan of Nilakantheshwar Mahadev. In this VIP darshan tradition the officer goes straight to the sanctum. Perhaps interest in history makes him pause briefly to view the temple's fine architecture. Hardly any collector notices the neglect around the temple. No one will have gone into Udaipur's lanes, where a thousand years of known history peeps from every ruin, building and doorway.

reject_reason: general commentary on bureaucratic neglect; no specific evidence
